What to remember?: Edit and reinforce memories after the fact

Definition: Spaced practice improves long-term memory more than cramming.
Example:
1. Studying weekly remembers more than one-night cramming.
 2. Reviewing vocabulary over days improves recall.
 3. Practicing piano daily beats one long session.
 4. Revisiting notes weekly strengthens retention.
 5. Spaced quizzes improve exam performance. 

1. Bahrick et al. (1993): 13 spaced sessions (56-day gaps) matched 26 massed sessions for 9-year vocabulary retention.
2. Rohrer & Taylor (2006): College students' 4-week math test scores nearly doubled with distributed vs. massed practice.
3. Taylor & Rohrer (2008): Spaced geometry practice produced 78% vs. 38% on delayed tests.
4. Sobel et al. (2011): One-week spacing outperformed massed learning in real fifth-grade classrooms.
5. Cumulative final exams force spaced learning and boost long-term retention.
Counter Example:
Cramming helps short-term recall before test.
One session suffices for simple facts.
Repetition without gaps still works briefly.
Single intensive workshop teaches basic skills.
Immediate practice boosts temporary performance.

1. Massed practice (cramming) outperforms spacing when tests are taken immediately after the study session.
2. Wiseheart et al. (2017): No spacing effect found in piano learning for a 17-note sequence or song accuracy across different lag intervals.
3. Some preschool-age children don't show spacing benefits, though recent research suggests they may still benefit.
4. Spacing fails with paraphrased repetitions (changed surface structure) and under lengthy lag conditions.
5. One classroom study found no benefit of spacing for children in grades 2-6, though the "massed" condition may have been spread across multiple days.

Definition: Memories change due to leading questions or suggestions.
Example:
After being asked how fast the cars were going when they “smashed,” witnesses later remember broken glass that never existed.
 A child repeatedly asked, “Did the man touch you?” eventually recalls being touched, despite no such event occurring.
 An officer hints “we caught the guy,” leading a witness to confidently identify an innocent person.
 Parents tell a story about you getting lost as a toddler; years later, you vividly “remember” it — though it never happened.
 A therapist suggests childhood trauma, and over time the client forms detailed memories aligned with that suggestion.

* When people are asked how fast cars were going when they "smashed" into each other rather than "hit," they later remember seeing broken glass at the scene that was never there. (Loftus & Palmer, 1974) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/

* After being told repeatedly that a classroom visitor named Sam Stone was clumsy and careless, many preschoolers later reported watching him rip a book and dirty a teddy bear, even though he never touched either. (Leichtman & Ceci, 1995) https://honorshd101.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/02/leichtman-ceci-1995-memory-sam-stone.pdf

* When family members told participants they had gotten lost in a shopping mall as a young child, roughly a quarter of them later formed detailed memories of an event that their relatives confirmed never happened. (Loftus & Pickrell, 1995) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37017540/

* When surrounded by a room full of people who all give the same obviously wrong answer, about 37% of people go along with the group and say the same wrong thing even when they can see with their own eyes that it is incorrect. (Asch, 1951) https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/asch-conformity-experiments

* When an officer tells a witness after a lineup "you identified the right person," the witness later recalls having been far more certain and having had a much clearer view during the crime, even when they picked the wrong person. (Douglass & Steblay, 2006) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7937609/

* Patients who were told a sugar pill was a powerful painkiller reported genuinely feeling less pain, and brain scans showed real changes in the parts of the brain that process pain. (Colloca & Barsky, 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4211281/

* When people were told that the wine they were drinking cost $45 instead of $5, they rated its taste as significantly more enjoyable, and brain scans confirmed that the pleasure centers of their brains were actually more active. (Plassmann et al., 2008) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2242704/

* When some clients sought therapy for mental health struggles and therapists suggested their problems might stem from repressed childhood abuse, some clients subsequently developed detailed memories of abuse that had never occurred. (Otgaar et al., 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11835833/

* When teachers were told that certain randomly selected students were about to experience an intellectual growth spurt, those students showed significantly greater IQ gains by the end of the year than their peers. (Rosenthal & Jacobson, 1968) https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02322211

* Adolescents who regularly see friends and influencers on social media promoting certain eating habits or body ideals are more likely to adopt those same behaviors and perceptions about their own bodies. (Chung et al., 2021) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8212626/

* When students in one school reported strange symptoms like dizziness and nausea after believing they had been exposed to a toxic smell, the illness rapidly spread to dozens of other students even after investigators found no harmful substance in the building. (Bartholomew & Wessely, 2002) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC543940/

* When a doctor grimaces and says "this is going to hurt" before a routine injection, patients report significantly more pain than when the same procedure is described neutrally, because the suggestion shapes what they expect to feel. (Colloca et al., 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6909539/

* Young children who are asked the same question repeatedly during an interview tend to change their answer on subsequent asks, interpreting the repeated question as a signal that their first answer was wrong. (Ceci & Bruck, 1995) https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1133074015000124

* When suspects are subjected to long, pressured interrogations where investigators repeatedly hint they could not possibly have committed the crime, some innocent people eventually come to doubt their own memories and believe they may actually be guilty. (Gudjonsson, 2021) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7937609/

* A person who reads online that a supplement causes headaches is significantly more likely to report headaches after taking it than someone who was not given that information beforehand, even when the pill contains no active ingredient. (Häuser et al., 2012) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6381056/

* When people overhear a friend confidently misremember a detail about a shared event, they often update their own memory of the event to match the friend's version, even when their original memory was accurate. (Zaragoza et al., 2007) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10492197/

* People who score higher on tests of imaginative suggestibility are more likely to respond to nonhypnotic suggestions and to produce vivid mental experiences simply because someone tells them to imagine something in a certain way. (Braffman & Kirsch, 1999) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10510510/

* Younger children are substantially more susceptible to accepting false suggestions from an authority figure than older children or adults, meaning age is one of the strongest predictors of how easily someone's memory can be shaped by an outside source. (Ceci & Bruck, 1995) https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1133074015000124

* When a friend insists you loved a movie you actually felt lukewarm about, you may walk away genuinely remembering you enjoyed it, because social suggestion can quietly reshape even recent subjective experiences. (Loftus, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10492197/
Counter Example:
Neutral questions preserve original memories.
Independent recall resists suggestion.
Recording events reduces later distortion.
Multiple sources confirm consistent memories.
Careful interviewing avoids leading questions.

* When eyewitnesses are told before an interview that the information they are about to hear may not be reliable, they are significantly less likely to incorporate that misleading information into their memory of the original event. (Chan et al., 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7502729/

* When just one person in a group gives the correct answer instead of going along with the wrong majority, conformity rates drop by as much as 80%, showing that a single ally can almost entirely cancel out group pressure to accept a false suggestion. (Asch, 1956) https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/asch-conformity-experiments

* When engineering students in the UK were put through the same line-judgment task that produced 37% conformity in American students in the 1950s, only one out of 396 trials showed conformity, demonstrating that domain expertise and cultural context can block suggestibility almost entirely. (Perrin & Spencer, 1981) https://bpspsychub.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.2044-8309.1981.tb00533.x

* People with higher working memory capacity are consistently better at recognizing and rejecting misleading post-event information, meaning cognitive resources serve as a natural buffer against suggestibility. (Greene et al., 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11680610/

* Even people with extraordinarily detailed autobiographical memories, who can recall daily events from decades ago, are just as susceptible to suggestion and false memory formation as people with ordinary memory, showing that memory strength alone does not protect against suggestibility. (Patihis et al., 2013) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3876244/

* When participants pay close attention to an event and encode it with high visual salience, younger adults are significantly less likely to form false memories in response to misleading information about that event. (Fraisse et al., 2024) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12702595/

* When a witness is told that the person who provided them with post-event information was untrustworthy or incompetent, the misinformation effect is substantially reduced, showing that perceived source credibility determines whether a suggestion takes hold. (Dodd & Bradshaw, 1980; Zaragoza et al., 2007) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10492197/

* When people are taught about how human memory works and how easily it can be distorted, they show measurably lower rates of accepting false suggestions in subsequent eyewitness memory tests. (Szpitalak & Polczyk, 2019) https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-019-00490-9

* When a doctor describes a procedure using neutral or positive framing instead of leading with warnings about pain, patients report experiencing significantly less discomfort, showing that the nocebo effect depends on specific communication choices and can be avoided. (Colloca et al., 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6909539/

* A person who witnesses a car accident and tells no one about it before being questioned is much less likely to incorporate misleading details into their account than someone who discussed it with others first, because retelling creates new opportunities for suggestion to enter memory. (Zaragoza et al., 2007) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10492197/

* When older adults are asked about contradictory misinformation that directly conflicts with something they already know, they are actually less likely to accept it than younger adults, showing that life experience with a topic can resist certain types of suggestion. (Huff & Umanath, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5820229/

* A person who holds a strong prior belief, backed by personal experience, in a political or factual matter tends not to update that belief in response to casual social suggestion, because motivated reasoning acts as a shield against external influence. (Ecker et al., 2022) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12747692/

* When someone openly knows they are taking a sugar pill with no active ingredients, the placebo effect still occurs for symptoms like pain and fatigue, but it does not change biological markers like cholesterol, meaning suggestion only influences things the brain can modulate. (Kaptchuk et al., 2010) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6889847/

* When younger adults strongly encode the details of a witnessed event, they show little to no difference in false memory rates compared to older adults, meaning encoding strength can override age-related suggestibility differences. (Wylie et al., 2002) https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/canadian-journal-on-aging-la-revue-canadienne-du-vieillissement/article/abs/younger-adults-can-be-more-suggestible-than-older-adults-the-influence-of-learning-differences-on-misinformation-reporting/0E73CCFD5DFEF7612793507D07485323

* When people actively think about where information came from rather than just what it says, they are less likely to confuse a suggested detail with something they actually witnessed, because source monitoring acts as a mental check against suggestibility. (Lindsay & Johnson, 1989) https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/misinformation-effect

* Suggestibility toward nocebo effects is a trait that varies significantly between individuals, meaning a warning about side effects that triggers real symptoms in one person may have no effect at all on another person who scores low on suggestibility measures. (Colloca & Barsky, 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11662164/

* When a child is interviewed using open-ended, non-leading questions that do not imply a preferred answer, they are far more likely to report only what they actually remember, showing that the absence of suggestion is what keeps testimony accurate. (Ceci & Bruck, 1995) https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1133074015000124

* A mechanic who notices a car part looks wrong will not change their assessment just because a customer insists it is fine, because domain-specific expertise creates confidence in one's own judgment that resists social suggestion. (Perrin & Spencer, 1981) https://bpspsychub.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.2044-8309.1981.tb00533.x

* When people are shown that the source of a piece of misinformation had a conflict of interest or an ulterior motive, they substantially reduce their reliance on that suggestion even without receiving a direct correction of the false information. (Ecker et al., 2024) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11345350/

* When eyewitnesses answer questions privately rather than in the presence of others, they show significantly lower rates of conformity to incorrect information, because social pressure requires an audience to generate the discomfort that drives suggestibility. (Asch, 1956) https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/asch-conformity-experiments

Definition: Remembering events that never actually happened.
Example:
Recalling childhood event that never occurred.
 Remembering meeting someone never met.
 Believing you visited a place unvisited.
 Recalling words not presented in lists.
 Remembering imagined story as real.

I. Loftus (1970s): Participants exposed to misleading information about a car accident reported seeing broken glass and higher speeds when the question used "smashed" vs. "hit"
II. Loftus's "Lost in the Mall" study: 25% of participants developed false memories of being lost in a shopping mall as a child; a 2019 replication found 35%
III. Loftus et al. (1978): Participants shown a yield sign but told they saw a stop sign—the overlap made it easier to accept misinformation
IV. Loftus & colleagues: Misleading information can actually overwrite the original memory of an event, especially with increasing age
V. Misinformation effect research: Participants generally endorse misinformation quickly and with high confidence, qualifying as genuine false memory




* After studying a list of words all related to sleep, like "bed," "rest," and "dream," people confidently report having seen the word "sleep" on the list even though it was never there. (Roediger & McDermott, 1995) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5030226/

* When college students were told a false story about spilling punch at a wedding as a child and asked about it across multiple interviews, about 25% eventually developed detailed memories of an event that never happened. (Hyman et al., 1995) https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/acp.2350090302

* When family members told participants they had been lost in a shopping mall as a child, roughly a quarter of them formed vivid memories of an event their relatives confirmed never occurred. (Loftus & Pickrell, 1995) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37017540/

* When people were shown a digitally altered photo of themselves as a child in a hot air balloon, about half of them developed detailed personal memories of a ride that never took place. (Wade et al., 2002) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8373035/

* When participants asked to imagine a minor childhood event in detail, like accidentally breaking a window, their confidence that the event had really happened increased significantly compared to events they had not imagined. (Garry et al., 1996) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24213869/

* After being told as part of a study that they had gotten sick from eating strawberry ice cream as a child, up to 40% of participants came to believe this false memory and later said they did not want to eat that food. (Bernstein et al., 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8373035/

* When people were interviewed multiple times using suggestive techniques about a crime they had never committed, around 70% developed detailed false memories of committing assault or theft as a teenager. (Shaw & Porter, 2015) https://www.psychologicalscience.org/news/releases/people-can-be-convinced-they-committed-a-crime-they-dont-remember.html

* People who had been awake all night were significantly more likely than well-rested people to incorporate misleading post-event details into their memories of a witnessed event, showing that fatigue directly increases false memory formation. (Lo et al., 2016) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5324644/

* Students who wrote down their memory of hearing about the 9/11 attacks were just as likely to have inconsistent details months later as those who recorded an ordinary memory, showing that even vivid emotional memories become distorted over time. (Talarico & Rubin, 2003) https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1111/1467-9280.02453

* When people saw a news article about a hurricane alongside a photo of a damaged village, they falsely remembered the article mentioning more deaths and injuries than it actually described, showing that images can distort what we think we read. (Garry et al., 2007) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8373035/

* Participants who attended an event together and then discussed it with each other afterward often incorporated details mentioned by their companion into their own memory, even when those details were things only the other person had seen. (Meade & Roediger, 2002) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10829763/

* About 40% of students who were interviewed about the Challenger space shuttle disaster two and a half years after it happened gave accounts that contradicted what they had written the day after the explosion, yet rated their confidence in the later version as high. (Neisser & Harsch, 1992) https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1111/1467-9280.02453

* People sometimes remember turning off the stove or taking their medication because it is part of their usual routine, not because they actually have a clear memory of doing it that specific time, making routine actions especially prone to false memory. (Johnson et al., 1997) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1692093/

* When a witness overhears another witness describe a detail they did not see themselves, they frequently incorporate that detail into their own account and later recall it as something they personally witnessed. (Gabbert et al., 2003) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9095591/

* When people repeatedly imagined performing a simple action like flipping a coin, they later remembered having actually done it, showing that mental rehearsal can create false memories of actions that were only imagined. (Goff & Roediger, 1998) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3213001/

* A person who dreams vividly about a conversation with a friend may wake up genuinely believing the conversation happened, because the brain uses similar processes to store imagined and real experiences. (Johnson et al., 1997) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1692093/

* Even people with extraordinarily detailed autobiographical memories who can recall events from decades ago were just as likely as ordinary people to form false memories when shown misleading information in a study. (Patihis et al., 2013) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3876244/

* When people are asked misleading questions shortly after watching a film clip of a car accident, they later remember seeing things that were not in the film, like broken glass or a barn that was never there. (Loftus et al., 1978) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10492197/

* Children who were told four weeks before a classroom visit that a guest named Sam Stone was clumsy later reported seeing him rip a book and dirty a teddy bear during his visit, even though he had done neither. (Leichtman & Ceci, 1995) https://honorshd101.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/02/leichtman-ceci-1995-memory-sam-stone.pdf

* People who read heavily covered news stories and social media posts about events they did not personally witness often later confuse things they read about with things they actually saw, blurring the line between their memory and media consumption. (Schacter, 2021) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8373035/
Counter Example:
Verifying memories with photos and records.
Distinguishing imagination from actual experiences.
Cross-checking events with others’ accounts.
Using diaries to confirm past events.
Recognizing uncertainty in vague recollections.

I. Loftus (2005): Some people are resistant to misinformation effects under certain conditions, though the exact boundary conditions remain unclear
II. False memories fail when semantic similarity is weak—changing details that have no semantic relation to the original event produces minimal false memory effects
III. Okado & Stark (2005): Brain scans showed some individuals' neural activity patterns predicted they would resist misinformation, maintaining accurate memories
IV. Strong encoding of original events reduces susceptibility to false memories from later misinformation
V. Warnings about potential misinformation can reduce false memory formation in some studies


* When people are warned before an interview that some information they are about to hear may be inaccurate, they show significantly lower rates of incorporating that false information into their memories of the original event. (Chan et al., 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7502729/

* When someone correctly remembers that they did not take their medication this morning because they have a specific, distinctive memory of skipping it while rushing out the door, they are accurately tracking a real event rather than constructing a false one. (Johnson et al., 1997) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1692093/

* A skilled mechanic who correctly recalls that a car came in with a specific noise last Tuesday is demonstrating accurate memory for a distinctive and professionally relevant event, not a false memory. (Perrin & Spencer, 1981) https://bpspsychub.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.2044-8309.1981.tb00533.x

* When someone accurately remembers the main plot of a novel they read last year but forgets minor details like character names, this is normal memory decay and forgetting rather than a false memory, because no incorrect information has been added. (Schacter, 2021) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8373035/

* When participants were warned before a memory test that the word lists they had studied were designed to make them think of related words that were not actually on the list, they showed significantly reduced false recognition of those lure words. (Roediger & McDermott, 1995; Gallo, 2006) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.686390/full

* When people are shown a factual correction to something they read previously and told to stop relying on the original information, they can reduce their use of the incorrect information when forming judgments, even though the false memory influence is rarely eliminated entirely. (Ecker et al., 2010) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11345350/

* Implanting a false memory of receiving a painful medical procedure as a child was significantly harder than implanting a plausible false event like getting lost in a mall, showing that extremely implausible events do not easily become false memories. (Pezdek & Hodge, 1999) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5248593/

* A witness who correctly identifies a perpetrator in a lineup and maintains that identification consistently across multiple interviews is demonstrating a stable accurate memory, not a false memory, even though false memories can arise in similar situations. (Wells & Bradfield, 1998) https://www.innocenceproject.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/Steblay_Wells_Douglass_2014_PPPL.pdf

* When someone recalls a strongly emotional and personally significant event, like the birth of a child, with high accuracy across many years because they have thought and talked about it frequently, this is accurate autobiographical memory maintained through rehearsal rather than a false memory. (Talarico & Rubin, 2003) https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1111/1467-9280.02453

* When people are asked to monitor the source of information they are recalling, for example by asking whether a detail came from the original video or a later summary, they show reduced false memory errors because source monitoring counteracts false attribution. (Lindsay & Johnson, 1989) https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/misinformation-effect

* People with higher working memory capacity are better at rejecting misleading post-event details and keeping their original memory intact, showing that cognitive resources can prevent false memory formation under the right conditions. (Greene et al., 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11680610/

* When a child gives a consistent, unprompted, and spontaneous account of something that happened without being asked leading questions, they are demonstrating accurate recall rather than a false memory created by external suggestion. (Ceci & Bruck, 1995) https://www.sciencedirect.com/article/pii/S1133074015000124

* A person who forgets where they put their keys is experiencing normal forgetting, not a false memory, because they have not formed an incorrect memory of a specific wrong location to replace the correct one. (Schacter, 2001) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8373035/

* When participants in a study correctly rejected a word as not being on a list they studied, even when that word was semantically related to many words that were on the list, they were successfully using distinctive memory features to resist false recognition. (Gallo, 2006) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.686390/full

* When older adults are asked to remember events that directly contradict something they know from experience, they are actually less likely to accept those contradictory suggestions than younger adults, showing that some forms of life knowledge protect against false memory. (Huff & Umanath, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5820229/

* When people are trained on how memory works and taught to notice the difference between things they actually experienced and things they only heard about, they subsequently make fewer false memory errors in memory tests. (Szpitalak & Polczyk, 2019) https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-019-00490-9

* A trauma survivor who accurately and consistently recalls the key details of what happened to them across multiple accounts over time is demonstrating genuine memory, not a false memory, even though traumatic memories can sometimes be distorted. (Otgaar et al., 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11835833/

* When someone accurately remembers having already told a particular joke to a friend and stops themselves from repeating it, they are exercising successful source monitoring and accurate memory retrieval rather than experiencing a false memory. (Johnson et al., 1997) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1692093/

* When participants in a study correctly remembered details from a video they watched even after being exposed to misleading information about those details, they were maintaining accurate memories by successfully resisting misinformation rather than forming false ones. (Chan et al., 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7502729/

* When a person confidently and accurately recalls that a meeting was scheduled for Thursday and checks their calendar to confirm, they are using external verification to anchor their memory to reality rather than relying on reconstructive processes that could lead to error. (Johnson et al., 1997) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1692093/

Definition: Forgetting source, believing recalled idea is original.
Example:
A student repeats a clever argument in an essay, genuinely believing they invented it — it was from last week’s lecture.
 A songwriter creates a melody, later realizing it closely matches a song they heard months ago.
 Someone tells a funny story, convinced it’s theirs, but it actually came from a friend.
 A designer proposes a “new” logo concept that subconsciously copies something seen online.
 A writer pitches a plot idea, unaware it mirrors a novel they once read.

I. Brown & Murphy (1989): In group category tasks, people inadvertently plagiarized 3-9% of the time by regenerating another person's idea as their own
II. George Harrison's "My Sweet Lord": Faced legal consequences for subconsciously copying the melody despite a genuine belief it was original
III. Helen Keller: Inadvertently borrowed from a story read to her years earlier, leading to plagiarism accusations
IV. Nietzsche case (analyzed by Jung): Likely unconsciously integrated material encountered decades earlier from Burckhardt's work into his philosophical writing
V. Marsh & Bower (1994): Word-search puzzle task showed substantially higher cryptomnesia rates (3-5%) than earlier category studies, manipulated by retention interval and encoding depth



* When participants in a group brainstorming task were later asked to come up with new ideas in the same category, they repeated ideas suggested by other group members between 3 and 9 percent of the time while genuinely believing those ideas were their own. (Brown & Murphy, 1989) https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/psych/people/fsch/fsch/studentresources/3rdyearprojects/projects/plag2.pdf

* When people competed against a computer partner in a word-search puzzle and were later asked to find new words, they regularly produced words the computer had already found and presented them as original, showing that cryptomnesia occurs even in simple problem-solving tasks. (Marsh & Bower, 1993) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8501434/

* When participants were put under time pressure to generate new ideas quickly, they plagiarized significantly more of their partners' previous ideas than when they had time to think, because speeded responding prevents the source-monitoring check that stops idea theft. (Marsh et al., 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232448515_Contributions_of_Inadequate_Source_Monitoring_to_Unconscious_Plagiarism_During_Idea_Generation

* George Harrison sincerely believed he composed "My Sweet Lord" from scratch, but a court found in 1976 that the melody was unconsciously copied from "He's So Fine" by the Chiffons, a song he had heard years earlier and forgotten. (Bright Tunes Music v. Harrisongs Music, 1976) https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/law/former-beatle-george-harrison-loses-plagiarism-lawsuit

* Helen Keller wrote a short story at age eleven that closely mirrored a fairy tale she had been read four years earlier and had no memory of, genuinely believing she had invented the entire story herself. (Taylor, 1965; Wikipedia on Cryptomnesia) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptomnesia

* A person who hears a clever phrase during a conversation and uses it two weeks later in a meeting as if they thought of it on the spot is experiencing cryptomnesia, because the content of the idea outlasted the memory of where it came from. (Marsh et al., 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232448515_Contributions_of_Inadequate_Source_Monitoring_to_Unconscious_Plagiarism_During_Idea_Generation

* When ideas were generated in a more anonymous group setting rather than in a one-on-one exchange, participants were more likely to claim others' ideas as their own, because the larger social context made it harder to track which person had said what. (Marsh et al., 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232448515_Contributions_of_Inadequate_Source_Monitoring_to_Unconscious_Plagiarism_During_Idea_Generation

* When participants were induced into a happy mood before a word puzzle task, they made significantly more source errors and claimed more of their partner's answers as their own than participants who were in a sad or neutral mood. Citing sources for recalled ideas.
Checking originality before claiming ideas.
Tracking references during note-taking.
Acknowledging possible prior exposure.
Verifying novelty through research.

II. Cryptomnesia rates drop when people actively monitor for sources during creative tasks

V. Increased encoding difficulty and shorter retention intervals reduce cryptomnesia plagiarism rates

* When participants were held accountable for the originality of their responses by being told their contributions would be individually evaluated, rates of unconscious plagiarism decreased significantly compared to participants in anonymous group conditions. * A researcher who keeps detailed notes and citations during a literature review and correctly attributes each idea to its source when writing a paper is using deliberate source-monitoring strategies that prevent cryptomnesia from occurring. (McCabe, 2008) https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/BF03193444

* A person who hears an idea in a meeting and immediately writes down the name of the person who said it alongside the idea itself is engaging in active source tagging that makes cryptomnesia far less likely when they revisit their notes later. * Someone who reads a book, puts it down, and then remembers weeks later that the book was where they first encountered a particular idea is engaging in successful source recall, the opposite of cryptomnesia. (Johnson et al., 1997) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1692093/

* When participants were tested immediately after a group idea-generation task, they showed substantially lower rates of plagiarism than those tested a week later, demonstrating that a strong, recent memory of the source is what prevents cryptomnesia. Definition: Misremembering where information was originally learned.
Example:
Attributing news to friend, actually read online.
 Believing teacher said fact, from textbook.
 Thinking rumor came from reliable source.
seeing a  movie changing memories of your childhood.
 Attributing quote to wrong person.

I. Ronald Reagan (cited in Johnson et al. 1993): Retold a story from a 1940s Dan Andrews movie as if it were an official Army report
II. George W. Bush: Recalled seeing live footage of the 9/11 attacks on TV, despite no live footage being broadcast at that time
III. Johnson & Raye (1979): People confuse imagined scenarios with actual perceptions, especially when both have similar perceptual vividness
IV. Johnson, Hashtroudi & Lindsay (1993): Participants misattributed newly presented words to having mentally generated them earlier
V. Misleading suggestions cause people to believe they witnessed things they only read or heard about in a courtroom setting
Counter Example:
Noting sources when learning information.
Checking origins before sharing claims.
Keeping citations for facts.
Verifying information with original sources.
Separating fiction from real events.

I. Johnson & Raye (1981) introduced reality monitoring: People can successfully discriminate internal events (thoughts, imaginations) from external perceived events under normal conditions
II. High confidence in initial encoding prevents source confusion in many cases
III. Distinctive perceptual details help maintain source separation—confusions occur primarily with ambiguous or overlapping sources
IV. Item memory and source memory are dissociated—people often retain accurate item information while confusing its source
V. Explicit source labeling at encoding significantly reduces source confusion errors

Definition: Correct memory assigned to wrong source or cause.
Example:
Remembering face, misidentifying where seen.
 Attributing idea to wrong colleague.
 Linking emotion to incorrect event.
 Recognizing person from wrong context.
 You recall feeling anxious and blame a test, when it was really lack of sleep.

I. Schacter (1999): People vividly recall hearing facts in conversations when they were actually read in texts, mixing up sources of information
II. Loftus eyewitness testimony: Witnesses confidently identify perpetrators based on memories distorted through suggestion or misinformation
III. Johnson & colleagues: People confuse imagined events with real perceptions, especially when both have similar sensory detail
IV. Source confusion in dreams: People misattribute details from dreams to actual experiences they witnessed
V. Post-event misinformation effect: Participants believe they saw details they only read or heard about later in the event sequence
Counter Example:
Confirming source before attributing memories.
Cross-checking recollections with timelines.
Asking others to verify sources.
Keeping records of information origins.
Reflecting on context during recall.

I. Johnson & Raye (1981) reality monitoring: People can successfully discriminate internal events from external perceived events under normal conditions
II. Strong perceptual encoding prevents misattribution—vivid, distinctive memories resist source confusion
III. Reality checks and deliberate source monitoring significantly reduce misattribution errors
IV. Explicit source labeling during encoding prevents misattribution of memories
V. Young, healthy individuals show fewer misattribution errors than older adults or those with neurological damage

Definition: Negative emotions fade faster than positive memories.
Example:
1. Remembering vacation joy, forgetting travel stress.
 2. Laughing about past embarrassment later.
 3. Recalling praise, downplaying earlier criticism.
 4. Fondly recalling school, ignoring exam anxiety.
 5. Remembering wins more than painful losses.

I. Walker et al. (1997): Emotions of autobiographical memories fade over time with unpleasant emotions fading faster than pleasant emotions
II. Gibbons et al. (2011): Negative memories and associated emotions begin to fade within 12 hours of the event
III. Walker et al. (2003): The Fading Affect Bias acts as a built-in healing process, helping people maintain pleasant lives
IV. Ritchie et al. (2015): Negative affect fades more quickly from episodic memory than positive affect across various populations
V. Landau & Gunter (2009): The FAB occurs regardless of whether experiences are individual memories or shared group memories
Counter Example:
1. Trauma memories retain strong negative emotion.
 2. Replaying failures with lasting distress.
 3. Negative events remembered vividly long-term.
 4. Journaling preserves negative emotions accurately.
 5. Therapy processing keeps emotional impact salient.

I. Ritchie et al. (2019): Individuals with eating disorder symptoms show diminished or absent FAB, losing the protective effect of fading negative emotions
II. Depressed individuals show reduced or reversed FAB, perceiving their lives as more negative than they actually are
III. Trait anxiety reduces affective fading for both positive and negative autobiographical memories
IV. High rehearsal of negative memories prevents the fading affect bias from occurring
V. Ritchie et al. (2009): When participants rehearse or ruminate about negative events, they do not show normal FAB patterns

Definition: Negative events weigh more than positive ones.
Example:
1. Remembering insults more than compliments.
 2. Focusing on one mistake among successes.
 3. Bad review outweighs many good reviews.
 4. Noticing criticism over praise at work.
 5. Remembering failures more than achievements.

I. Baumeister et al. (2001): Negative events, emotions, feedback, and information are universally more powerful than positive counterparts across nearly every domain
II. Feedback ratio: A single piece of negative feedback requires approximately 3 to 5 positive pieces to neutralize its psychological impact
III. Baumeister et al.: Negative interactions carry substantially more weight than positive ones in determining relationship satisfaction
IV. Kensinger (2007): Negative stimuli attract more attention and are remembered better than positive stimuli in younger adults
V. Learning research: Punishment for incorrect responses is more effective at enhancing learning than rewards for correct responses
Counter Example:
1. Gratitude practice highlights positive experiences.
 2. Balanced feedback considers positives and negatives.
 3. Deliberately recalling daily successes.
 4. Weighing evidence equally across outcomes.
 5. Positive reframing reduces negative dominance.

I. Matlin & Stang (1978): Well over 100 findings from various paradigms show a positivity bias in autobiographical recall, especially for early childhood memories
II. Short-term memory shows advantages for positive information over negative information in some contexts
III. Positive mood states can reduce or reverse negativity bias in decision-making
IV. Personal success experiences often show stronger memory retention than failure experiences in some studies
V. Evolutionary adaptation: In safe, resource-rich environments, positivity bias may emerge as people focus less on threat detection

Definition: Prejudging people based on group membership.
Example: 1. Distrusting someone because of their background. 2. Avoiding classmates from unfamiliar groups. 3. Assuming abilities based on group identity. 4. Judging character from appearance alone. 5. Expecting behavior based on stereotypes.
Counter Example: 1. Evaluating individuals by personal actions. 2. Seeking diverse friendships intentionally. 3. Challenging assumptions with evidence. 4. Learning about different cultures. 5. Reflecting before forming judgments.

Example: I. Allport (1954): Prejudice emerges from minimal group categorization and intergroup contact threat perception. II. Sherif et al. (1961): Superordinate goals requiring cooperation can reduce prejudicial attitudes between groups. III. Pettigrew & Tropp (2006): Intergroup contact under optimal conditions significantly reduces prejudice across multiple contexts. IV. Dovidio et al. (1997): Prejudicial attitudes persist through automatic cognitive associations even when explicit beliefs change. V. Turner (1987): Social identity theory demonstrates that group membership automatically triggers ingroup favoritism and outgroup derogation.
Counter Example: I. Allport (1954): Optimal conditions for contact include equal status, cooperative goals, and authority support for desegregation. II. Gaertner et al. Hewstone & Brown (1986): Learning counterstereotypical information about individuals can gradually modify group-level prejudices.

Definition: Applying stereotypes to judge individuals inaccurately.
Example: 1. Assuming profession from appearance. 2. Expecting skills based on group labels. 3. Predicting behavior using stereotypes. 4. Overgeneralizing from one group member. 5. Judging competence by accent.

Counter Example: I. Wilder (1984): Repeated exposure to stereotype-disconfirming individuals reduces stereotype strength at both individual and group levels. II. Weber & Crocker (1983): Subtyping processes can isolate disconfirming individuals as exceptions rather than changing group stereotypes. III. Bless & Schwarz (1992): Processing stereotype-inconsistent information more carefully can lead to stereotype revision. V. Kunda et al. (2002): Implicit theories about group malleability influence whether people apply or revise stereotypes in response to counterevidence.

Definition: Best recall for the first items.
Example: 1. The first concept explained shaped my understanding of the entire topic. 2. I remembered the opening names from roll call better than later ones. 3. Definition: Being shown some items impairs recall of others.
Example: 1. Provided hints actually blocked my memory of other list items. 2. Partial reminders interfered with recalling the rest independently. 3. Example: I. Slamecka (1968): Providing retrieval cues for part of a study list reduces recall of the remaining uncued list items. II. Tulving (1974): Part-list cueing interference occurs because cues strategically retrieve related information at the expense of uncued items. III. Anderson et al. (1994): Retrieval-induced forgetting demonstrates that activating cued memories suppresses activation of related but non-cued memories. IV. Roediger (1973): The part-list cueing effect increases with list length and semantic relatedness between cued and uncued items. V. MacLeod et al. (2003): Part-list cueing effects are larger when cued and uncued items share category membership or semantic associations.
Counter Example: I. Raaijmakers & Shiffrin (1981): Part-list cueing effects are reduced when uncued items are from a different semantic category than cues. II. Amorim & Johnson (2005): Part-list cueing effects are minimal when participants retrieve uncued items in a different order than presentation.

Definition: Active suppression of unwanted memories.
Example: 1. To focus, I pushed unwanted thoughts out of awareness. 2. I deliberately suppressed the embarrassing memory during the presentation. 3. I tried not to think about the mistake, reducing its recall. 4. Suppressing the image helped me concentrate on studying. 5. I recalled the last spoken items better than the written ones.

Anderson & Green (2001): The think/no-think paradigm demonstrates that suppressing retrieval of specific memories reduces their subsequent recall. III. Depue et al. (2006): Prefrontal cortex activation during memory suppression correlates with reduced hippocampal memory trace reactivation. IV. Benoit & Anderson (2012): Memory suppression involves inhibitory control mechanisms that reduce memory trace accessibility. V. Levy & Anderson (2008): Suppression effectiveness depends on individuals' ability to divert attention from suppressed items.
Counter Example: I. Hertel & Calcaterra (2005): Suppression effects are reduced when retrieved memories are not emotionally significant or threatening. II. Bjork & Bjork (1996): Retrieval practice can overcome suppression effects through reconsolidation. III. Sahakyan & Delaney (2003): Context change reduces suppression effects by providing alternative retrieval pathways. IV. Hultin et al. (2016): Suppression effectiveness depends on executive function capacity; lower capacity individuals show weaker inhibition. V. Tomlinson et al. (2009): Motivation to suppress moderates inhibitory effectiveness; ambivalent motivation reduces suppression.

Definition: Auditory lists yield better recall of final items.
Example: 1. Auditory instructions stuck longer than the same list read silently. 2. Hearing the list improved recall of its ending. 3. Spoken directions were easier to remember than printed notes. 4. Listening to items increased recall of final items compared to reading. 5. Spoken presentations improved recall of the ending.

Penney (1989): Auditory modality produces a larger recency effect than visual modality through advantages in phonological short-term storage. III. Neath (1997): Auditory modality effects are larger when items are presented at normal speech rates versus accelerated rates. IV. Saito et al. (1992): Retrieval practice reduces list-length effects through strengthening of memory traces. III. (2008): Bayesian methods show some individuals maintain stable recall despite list length through different encoding strategies. V. Vergauwe et al. (2010): List-length effects can be eliminated through consolidation procedures that transfer items to long-term memory.

Definition: Recalling items in exact presented order.
Example: 1. I struggled because the test required recalling items in exact order. 2. Remembering steps sequentially was harder than recall. 3. Order errors ruined my serial recall performance. 4. I knew the items but forgot their correct order. 5. The phone number had to be recalled in precise sequence.
Counter Example: 1. Free recall: any order. 2. Cued recall: ignores sequence. 3. Recognition: identify items. 4. Category recall: ignores sequence. 5. Reconstruction: different task.

Example: I. Henson et al. (1996): Serial recall requires maintenance of positional information along with item identity, increasing task difficulty. II. Lewandowsky & Farrell (2008): Recall of sequence depends on both memory for items and memory for their ordinal positions. III. Brown et al. (2000): The primacy and recency effects in serial recall reflect distinct mechanisms for first and last items. IV. Page & Norris (1998): Serial recall errors show position-specific patterns reflecting interference between similar-position items across trials. V. Nairne (2002): Temporal context provides retrieval cues for serial recall; items encoded with temporal markers are recalled more accurately.
Counter Example: I. Free recall eliminates sequence requirements, producing substantially higher recall rates than serial recall. II. Cued recall—providing category cues—shows that item memory exceeds sequence memory in most contexts. III. Recognition testing shows individuals can identify items they cannot recall in correct serial order. IV. Retroactive inhibition affects serial order encoding less than it affects free recall. V. Reconstruction tasks that don't require serial order show higher accuracy than serial recall of identical items.

Definition: Duration has little effect on remembered evaluation.
Example: 1. I can evaluate duration focusing on moments instead. 2. Constant intensity matters; duration matters. 3. A billing error for hours duration matters less than the error itself. 4. My evaluation focused on the moment rather than how long it lasted. 5. Very short pain lasting long time felt less impactful.
Counter Example: 1. Can estimate duration when asked. 2. Constant intensity: duration matters. 3. Billing hours: duration primary. 4. Narrative accounts: duration shapes memory. 5. Very long pain more impactful.

Example: I. Kahneman et al. (1993): Remembered utility depends primarily on peak and end intensity rather than total duration of an experience. II. Ariely & Carmon (2000): Duration of pain has minimal effect on retrospective pain evaluations compared to peak pain and ending pain. III. Schreiber & Kahneman (2000): Aggregate duration has negligible influence on remembered satisfaction; ending intensity dominates judgments. IV. Redelmeier & Kahneman (1996): Patients' retrospective pain judgments correlate strongly with peak pain and final pain, not total duration. V. Do et al. (2008): Duration neglect appears robust across multiple stimulus types—pain, pleasure, sound, video—in remembered evaluation.
Counter Example: I. Cavanaugh et al. (2015): When explicitly asked to estimate duration, participants show accurate duration judgments despite neglecting duration in immediate evaluation. II. Kemp et al. (2008): Repeated experiences or vivid memories restore duration effects in older adults with preserved cognitive function. III. De Vries et al. (2012): Actively thinking about duration during experience reduces duration neglect in subsequent evaluation. IV. Mitchell et al. (2011): Billing hours: duration primary factor when payment depends on time rather than intensity. V. Zauberman & Urminsky (2016): Duration effects emerge when memory is probed weeks later; initial evaluation neglects duration.

Definition: Misleading info impairs original memory.
Example: 1. After hearing misleading information, I misremembered seeing details. 2. False information blended into my original memory. 3. Leading comments distorted my recall of the accident. 4. Post-event rumors reshaped my memory of the event. 5. Over time, I forgot minor details and exaggerated the main conflict.
Counter Example: 1. Detailed source monitoring reduces effect. 2. Central details resist misinformation. 3. Source tagged unreliable reduces effect. 4. Warnings mitigate effect. 5. Sleep-guided memory resists.

Example: I. Loftus et al. (1978): Exposure to post-event misinformation systematically distorts memory for the original event in predictable directions. II. Tversky & Kahneman (1974): Misleading questions bias subsequent memory reports toward suggested information. III. Loftus (2005): Misinformation effects are stronger when original memory traces are weak and misinformation is encountered soon after the event. IV. Mitchell et al. (2011): False memories created through misinformation persist despite repeated warnings about their unreliability. V. Frenda et al. (2016): Emotionally significant events show reduced misinformation effects compared to neutral events.
Counter Example: I. Johnson et al. (1993): Detailed source monitoring of original event details resists misinformation effects. II. Chambers et al. (2005): Central details involving action resist misinformation effects more than peripheral details. III. Skagerberg & Wright (2009): Instructing participants about misinformation likelihood before exposure reduces subsequent effect. IV. Ecker et al. (2010): Corrections and warnings substantially reduce misinformation effects when provided immediately. V. Payne et al. (1994): Sleep-dependent consolidation reduces susceptibility to misinformation presented after learning.

Definition: Memory loses details, exaggerates others.
Example: 1. The story became simpler with key points emphasized. 2. Retelling smoothed details and amplified emotional parts. 3. I lost nuance but sharpened emotional impact. 4. Immediate detailed report captures more than recall later. 5. I lost nuance but sharpened emotional impact.
Counter Example: 1. Moment-by-moment rating correlates better. 2. Multiple independent capture contradicts effect. 3. Detailed documentation stabilizes memory. 4. Ambiguous omission or realistic consolidation. 5. Objective outcomes not feeling.

Example: I. Bartlett (1932): Reproductions of stories show systematic changes over retelling with details leveled and emotionally significant elements sharpened. II. Wynn & Logie (1998): Narrative memory shows progressive simplification of peripheral details while central emotional elements remain vivid. III. Davis & Loftus (2007): Retelling of autobiographical narratives produces systematic leveling of trivial details and sharpening of consequential events. IV. Bergman & Roediger (1999): Repeated retrievals of autobiographical memories show progressive integration and emotional elaboration. V. Anderson & Ronnberg (1997): Leveling effects are stronger for details rated as less central to the narrative theme.
Counter Example: I. Accuracy maximization: Contemporaneous written records show minimal leveling and sharpening compared to retrospective recall. II. Multiple independent witnesses: Detailed independent accounts reduce systematic sharpening of consistent elements. III. Recorded documentation: Video or audio records reveal that memory narratives oversimplify compared to actual events. IV. Cognitive interview techniques: Reconstructing context reduces sharpening of emotional but not objective details. V. Autobiographical expertise: Individuals trained in detailed reporting show less dramatic leveling and sharpening.

Definition: Judgment based on peak and end moments.
Example: 1. I judged the vacation by its best moment and ending. 2. The painful procedure felt tolerable because it ended gently. 3. I remembered the peak excitement and conclusion. 4. The experience's ending outweighed average quality. 5. I remembered the peak excitement and conclusion.
Counter Example: 1. Moment-by-moment rating correlates better. 2. Multiple peaks debilitate rule application. 3. Ambiguous and hard to apply. 4. Objective outcomes not feeling. 5. Post-experience reflection; different rating.

Example: I. Kahneman et al. (2006): Remembered utility depends primarily on peak emotional intensity and end-state intensity rather than average utility throughout. II. Redelmeier & Kahneman (1996): Patients' remembered suffering correlates strongly with peak pain and final pain intensity, not total pain duration. III. Ariely & Carmon (2000): Adding a brief painful extension to the end of an experience paradoxically increases remembered positivity when pain level decreases. IV. Varey & Kahneman (1992): Peak-end rule predicts remembered satisfaction better than average or total utility in multiple domains. V. Fredrickson et al. (1993): The disproportionate influence of endings on retrospective evaluation appears automatic and implicit.
Counter Example: I. Tract recording: Contemporaneous moment-by-moment ratings of utility diverge substantially from peak-end predictions. II. Ariely & Zauberman (2003): When multiple equally intense peaks occur, the rule predicts poorly; averaging performs better. III. Experienced utility: Individuals making real-time choices frequently violate peak-end predictions and prioritize average utility. IV. Schreiber & Kahneman (2000): Objective outcome measures show weak correlation with peak-end model predictions. V. Mitchell et al. (2011): Delay between experience and judgment reduces peak-end effects; retrospective construction plays less role with delay.

Definition: Feeling you know a word but can't retrieve it.
Example: 1. I knew the actor's name but couldn't retrieve it. 2. The word imminent, not immediate, hovered just beyond reach. 3. I experienced a strong feeling of knowing without actual recall. 4. The answer hovered just beyond reach. 5. Slips of tongue, not feeling.
Counter Example: 1. Effortless recall: "apple." 2. Complete guessing, not feeling. 3. Rhyme cue retrieves word. 4. Sleep promotes retrieval. 5. Contextual priming eliminates state.

Example: I. Brown & McNeill (1966): Tip-of-the-tongue states occur when semantic knowledge is intact but phonological retrieval is temporarily blocked. II. Schwartz et al. (2000): TOT states involve high-confidence knowledge combined with retrieval failure; accuracy of guesses exceeds chance. III. Metcalfe (1993): Partial retrieval of related words accompanies TOT states, suggesting partial activation of target word. IV. Harley & Brown (1998): TOT states are more common for rare words with longer phonological forms. V. James & Burke (2000): TOT frequency increases with normal aging despite stable semantic knowledge.
Counter Example: I. Completely novel or learned facts: No TOT feeling; either retrieved or truly inaccessible. II. Extended cueing: Providing complete cues (rhymes, first letters) shows true retrieval versus blocking. III. Sleep consolidation: Delayed recall eliminates TOT states for many words. IV. Implicit priming: Context priming removes TOT by facilitating retrieval pathways. V. Encoding strength: Strongly encoded material shows no TOT; weak encoding produces blocked access without TOT.

Definition: Forgetting info available online.
Example: 1. I didn't memorize facts, knowing I could search it later. 2. Easy access reduced my effort to remember details. 3. I forgot information because it's stored digitally. 4. Search engines replaced my need to memorize facts. 5. Online availability made memorization unnecessary.
Counter Example: 1. Memorize own SSN or birthdate. 2. Memorize critical procedures. 3. Use memory techniques intentionally. 4. Remember non-searchable conversation. 5. No internet; better memory for info.

Example: I. Sparrow et al. (2011): Individuals preferentially store location information about where facts can be found rather than the facts themselves when internet access is assumed available. II. Henkel (2014): Knowing information will be available reduces encoding effort and subsequent memory for that information. III. Ward (2013): Memory for information available online shows reduced capacity compared to information believed unavailable. IV. Sungur & Spector (2015): Students who expect to access information later show reduced encoding and retention compared to students expecting to rely on memory. V. Fisher et al. (2015): Internet availability affects what information people choose to remember—facts versus locations—based on accessibility.
Counter Example: I. Distinctive expertise: Individuals trained in memorization techniques retain information despite online availability. II. Memorization skills: Professional memorizers show superior retention independent of internet access. III. Use memory techniques: Deliberate encoding strategies eliminate Google effect. IV. Remember conversations: Information from conversation resists Google effect because it's not easily searchable. V. Memory training: Loci method and other techniques produce retention despite belief in online availability.

Definition: Poor memory for person right before your turn.
Example: 1. A candidate prepares their reply, forgetting the interviewer's question. 2. A presenter focuses on their turn and misses earlier points. 3. I was so focused on my presentation that I missed what was said. 4. Participant tunes out while waiting to speak. 5. Tested on all later, no effect.
Counter Example: 1. Unexpected presentation: equal attention. 2. Unpredicatable targets: equal attention. 3. Prior info needed for your turn. 4. Testing on all later, no effect. 5. Tested on all prior, no effect.

Example: I. Brenner et al. (1996): Individuals show systematically poorer recall for information presented immediately before their turn to speak in group settings. II. Baddeley et al. (2009): The next-in-line effect reflects self-directed attention focused on planning upcoming contribution rather than encoding others' information. III. Jones et al. (1994): Memory for preceding speakers is worse when individuals must prepare a verbal response compared to passive listening. IV. Mazzoni & Nelson (1995): The effect is larger when individuals are internally focused on preparation rather than monitoring group interaction. V. Beaman et al. (2002): The effect is eliminated when individuals have no upcoming turn or know their turn will not require speaking.
Counter Example: I. Unexpected presentation: When the turn order is random or unknown, next-in-line effects are eliminated. II. Predictability: When speakers don't know they'll be called on, attention remains distributed equally. III. Prior information needed: When earlier speakers' information is essential for your turn, attention remains on the group. IV. Passive observation: Individuals not expecting to speak show equal attention to all speakers regardless of turn proximity. V. Recorded memory: When post-hoc testing occurs, no effect appears; initial attention capture explains the immediate effect.

Definition: Memory lapse due to inattention or automation.
Example: 1. Intentional focus during task aids memory. 2. Forgetting due to brain injury. 3. Always knowing where you left your car. 4. Error learning new complex task. 5. Deliberately not performing action.
Counter Example: 1. Intentional focus during task aids memory. 2. Forgetting due to brain injury. 3. Always knowing where you left your car. 4. Error learning new complex task. 5. Deliberately not performing action.

Example: I. Reason & Mycielska (1982): Absent-minded errors reflect failures of attention during automatic task performance, not retrieval failure. II. Norman (1981): Memory lapses from absent-mindedness occur during habitual actions where intention and execution become decoupled. III. Schachter (1999): Absent-mindedness reflects inattention to encoding rather than impaired retrieval mechanisms. IV. Baddeley (2003): Attentional lapses produce absent-minded errors by diverting cognitive resources from necessary monitoring. V. Craik & Lockhart (1972): Shallow encoding during automatic task performance produces absent-minded failures at retrieval.
Counter Example: I. Intentional encoding: Deliberate focus during encoding substantially reduces absent-minded lapses. II. Divided attention recovery: Redirecting attention to tasks reduces absent-minded error rates. III. Prospective memory support: External aids and reminders completely eliminate absent-minded lapses. IV. Expertise and attention: Practiced experts show fewer absent-minded errors through enhanced monitoring. V. Sleep-dependent consolidation: Well-consolidated memories show reduced absent-minded lapses even during distraction.

Definition: Deeper, meaningful processing improves memory.
Example: 1. Distinctive visual feature remembered well. 2. Deep but irrelevant processing fails. 3. Effortful shallow processing yields good memory. 4. Amnesic patients only shallow possible. 5. Implicit test: shallow equals deep.
Counter Example: 1. Distinctive visual feature remembered well. 2. Deep but irrelevant processing fails. 3. Effortful shallow processing yields good memory. 4. Amnesia patients only shallow possible. 5. Implicit test: shallow equals deep.

Example: I. Craik & Lockhart (1972): Thinking about what a word means produces deeper encoding and substantially better memory than thinking about its physical appearance. II. Craik & Tulving (1975): Semantic processing produces memory advantages that persist across retention intervals and interference. III. Rogers et al. (1977): When asked to rate words as describing themselves, participants show enhanced retention due to personal semantic elaboration. IV. Slamecka & Graf (1978): Semantic processing superiority extends across recognition, recall, and relearning measures. V. PMC replication (2017): Students who studied by thinking about meaning achieved higher test scores than those reviewing word definitions.
Counter Example: I. Craik & Lockhart (1972): Effortful shallow processing—thinking repeatedly about physical features—can produce memory levels approximating meaningful processing. II. Goschke et al. (1994): Transfer-appropriate processing shows shallow encoding produces good memory when tests match encoding modality. III. Challis & Brodbeck (1992): Implicit memory tests show no advantage for semantic versus non-semantic processing, contrary to levels predictions. IV. Moscovitch & Craik (1976): Amnesic patients show preserved implicit memory for shallow tasks despite impaired semantic memory. V. Tulving et al. (1982): Recognition memory may not always show semantic advantages; context and familiarity can override processing depth.
